one_liner: FFmpeg's libswscale and libavfilter (scale, crop, convolution) run the vips-bench crop/resize/sharpen job about 2.1x faster than ImageMagick 7.
what_it_does: libswscale converts and resamples raw frames between pixel formats and sizes: sws_scale_frame(ctx, dst, src) on AVFrames, or the older sws_getContext()/sws_scale() pair. libavfilter chains filters such as crop, scale (which wraps libswscale) and convolution (a per-plane 3x3/5x5/7x7 or row/column kernel) into a graph that the ffmpeg CLI builds from a -vf string. The catalogued result times the ffmpeg command line with TIFF decode and encode, not a library call. It is not a drop-in for ImageMagick: there is no magick-style command language and no tiled-TIFF input.
how_it_is_fast: libswscale (the 7.1 'legacy' backend) is a separable two-pass scaler. Each input line is converted to a planar intermediate (hand-written SIMD for packed RGB24 to Y/UV in x86 input.asm), filtered horizontally with precomputed per-pixel taps into 15-bit samples (hscale8to15 kernels specialised by filter size, AVX2 versions in scale_avx2.asm), then combined vertically from a ring buffer of lines (yuv2planeX, AVX2 yuv2yuvX). The scale filter hands swscale the filter graph's thread count, so it runs slice-threaded. The convolution filter is slice-threaded too, and for 8-bit 3x3 kernels on x86-64 it uses the ff_filter_3x3_sse4 assembly kernel. Master adds a new graph-based swscale with chained 'ops' SIMD kernels, a JIT and a Vulkan SPIR-V backend, but swscale.h says these backends are auto-selected only with SWS_UNSTABLE.
when_to_use: Frames are already in an FFmpeg pipeline (decode, filter, encode) and you need resize, crop or format conversion without leaving libav*: libswscale is the standard choice there.

Batch command-line jobs on many-core x86-64 boxes where ImageMagick 7 is the current tool and the format is something FFmpeg reads (strip TIFF, PNG, JPEG, video frames). In the libvips table, ffmpeg 7.1.1 took 2.06 s versus 4.41 s for magick on a 16-core Threadripper PRO 3955WX, with about 160 MB less peak memory (1338 MB versus 1500 MB).
Pixel-format conversion between YUV and RGB families with many supported layouts (8-16 bit, planar and packed, alpha), where breadth matters more than the last factor of speed.
Simple fixed-kernel sharpen or blur on 8-bit planar data: the convolution filter's SSE4 3x3 path plus slice threading is cheap to use from a filter string.
when_not_to_use: Still-image batch processing where speed and memory matter most. In the same table libvips (vips-c 8.18) took 0.57 s and 94 MB against ffmpeg's 2.06 s and 1338 MB, and GraphicsMagick 1.4 matched ffmpeg (2.05 s).

High-quality resizing in a video pipeline: zimg's README reports a Lanczos FHD-to-UHD resize in 7.7 ms versus 15.2 ms for swscale 4.0.2 (i7-8565U), and libyuv-style converters beat swscale on YUV/RGB conversion.

RGB-exact or colour-managed image work. Filters that accept only planar formats force hidden conversions, and with the vips-bench filter string the RGB image is converted to limited-range YUV 4:4:4 before the sharpen (see gotchas).
Tiled TIFF input: the benchmark had to feed ffmpeg a strip TIFF because its TIFF decoder does not read tiled TIFF (benchmark.sh comment).
Projects that cannot accept LGPL obligations, or builds configured with --enable-gpl (then GPL-2.0-or-later).

integration.form: shared or static libraries (libswscale, libavfilter, libavutil, plus libavcodec/libavformat for file I/O) built with FFmpeg's configure/make, or the ffmpeg CLI
integration.dependencies: libswscale needs only libavutil. libavfilter's scale filter needs libswscale. Reading and writing TIFF needs libavcodec and libavformat. The x86 SIMD sources are NASM-syntax .asm files, so an assembler is needed at build time to get the fast paths.
integration.min_toolchain: Not documented in the files read this session (FFmpeg's configure script sets the requirements).
integration.platforms: Any OS FFmpeg builds on. libswscale has SIMD directories for x86, aarch64, arm, loongarch, ppc and riscv, and master adds a Vulkan backend. On x86 the AVX2 horizontal scaler is skipped on CPUs flagged SLOW_GATHER (AMD family 0x19 and earlier, Intel Haswell-class), so the 3955WX in the benchmark ran the SSE-class hscale kernels.
integration.thread_safety: SwsContext has a threads field (0 = automatic) for internal slice threading. In libavfilter, slice threading follows the filter graph's thread count. Concurrent use of one SwsContext from several threads is not documented in the headers read.

gotchas: Hidden format conversion: in release/7.1, convolution accepts only planar formats (no packed RGB24), and the TIFF encoder accepts RGB24, RGBA, gray, PAL8 and planar YUV but not GBRP. Format negotiation therefore picks YUV444P as the closest common format to the RGB24 input (pick_format with av_find_best_pix_fmt_of_2), and the encoder declares limited-range YUV. The vips-bench command sharpens Y, Cb and Cr planes and writes a YCbCr TIFF, not an RGB one. Insert format=gbrp before convolution and convert back to rgb24 explicitly if you need RGB output, and check the choice with -loglevel debug ('picking ... out of').

Defaults differ from ImageMagick: the scale filter passes no flags, so libswscale uses its SWS_BICUBIC default. ffmpeg's TIFF encoder compresses with PackBits by default (compression_algo), while ImageMagick writes uncompressed TIFF here. Both add work on ffmpeg's side, so they do not inflate its result, but outputs are not byte-comparable.

Speed depends on CPU generation and backend: the AVX2 gather-based hscale is disabled on Zen 1-3 and Haswell, and the new swscale ops/JIT backends in master are used only with SWS_UNSTABLE ('may be faster, slower, or produce different output').
The GitHub repository is a read-only mirror. Its README says GitHub pull requests are ignored and patches go to the ffmpeg-devel mailing list, so do not look for bug reports or reviews there.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick FFmpeg when the data already lives in an FFmpeg decode/encode pipeline or you need its breadth of pixel formats. Pick libvips for still-image batch work (3.6x faster than ffmpeg in the same table with about a fourteenth of the peak memory, derived from page data). Pick zimg for higher-quality, faster resampling of video frames, and libyuv or yuv2rgb for raw YUV/RGB conversion.
verified_claims_summary: The libvips maintainers' Speed-and-memory-use table (AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04 packages, quickest real time of five runs, whole process including TIFF I/O) lists ffmpeg 7.1.1 at 2.06 s and 1338.36 MB peak against magick 7.1.1 at 4.41 s / 1500.52 MB and convert 4.44 s / 1499.29 MB, about 2.1x faster (derived from page data). Per the 7.1 code, the timed ffmpeg run is strip-TIFF decode, crop, swscale bicubic resize with RGB24 to YUV444P conversion, SSE4 3x3 sharpen on Y/Cb/Cr, and a PackBits YCbCr TIFF write, so it is not the same pixel pipeline as ImageMagick's RGB one.
status_note: Very active (last commit 2026-10-03, libswscale major version 10 on master with a new frame-based API). LGPL-2.1-or-later unless built with --enable-gpl. Usable as libraries, but too large to vendor piecemeal.
measurement_notes: Provenance flaw, not invalid evidence. vips-bench's ffmpeg.sh was first committed on 2025-09-21 ('add ffmpeg'), after the 12 Aug 2025 run date the wiki still gives, so that date does not cover the ffmpeg row. From 2025-09-21 until commit c4dbb24 on 2026-04-12, benchmark.sh called `./ffmpeg.sh $tmp/x-strip.tif -o $tmp/x2.tif`. Because ffmpeg.sh uses $1 and $2, ffmpeg would get '-o' as its last argument with no output file. release/7.1's option table (fftools/ffmpeg_opt.c) has no 'o' option, so split_commandline in cmdutils.c stops with "Unrecognized option 'o'" within milliseconds, and benchmark.sh's real_time() never checks exit status or output. The published 2.06 s therefore cannot have come from the committed driver of that period and was presumably run by hand. The 2026-04-12 commit fixed the call (and added -update true), yet the row still reads 2.06 s with the Aug 2025 date. The wiki revision diffs could not be read reliably here, so exactly when the row appeared is unconfirmed. Separately, my code reading (not a run) of release/7.1 format negotiation says the run sharpened limited-range YUV444P planes and wrote a PackBits YCbCr TIFF instead of an RGB TIFF, so the two pipelines do not produce equivalent output. Neither the RGB-to-YUV conversion nor PackBits makes ffmpeg's job lighter, so I see no inflation of the ratio. Threads: ffmpeg's filter graph defaults to automatic thread count, scale passes it to swscale, and convolution slices across it, while TIFF decode and encode stay single-threaded. On the Zen 2 test CPU the AVX2 hscale is skipped (SLOW_GATHER). Suggest keeping B with a documented shortcoming (driver mismatch and non-equivalent output) rather than a retier, unless the orchestrator wants C for the unreproducible provenance of the row.
